extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical geometry; mathematicians interested in Archimedean geometric proofs
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of geometric propositions and constructive proofs from Archimedes' On the Sphere and Cylinder, establishing relations between polygons, circles, cones, cylinders, surfaces and volumes by classical Euclidean methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polygon be circumscribed about a circle, the perimeter of the circumscribed polygon is greater than the perimeter of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via comparing each pair of adjacent sides meeting at a vertex A touching the circle at P and Q: PA + AQ > (arc PQ). A similar inequality holds for each angle; summing these inequalities yields the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal magnitudes, it is possible to find two unequal straight lines such that the greater straight line has to the less a ratio less than the greater magnitude has to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: given magnitudes AB (greater) and D, take BC along BA equal to D and an arbitrary GH; add C'A to itself repeatedly to exceed D to get AF, then choose GH so that GH is the same multiple of HF that AF is of AC. Using proportion inequalities (AC:AF < AC:CB) and componendo yields EG:GH < AB:D. The constructed GH, EG satisfy the condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal magnitudes and a circle, it is possible to inscribe a polygon in the circle and to describe another about it so that the side of the circumscribed polygon may have to the side of the inscribed polygon a ratio less than that of the greater magnitude to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Prop. 2 to find two straight lines with required ratio; construct right-angled triangle LMK with KM equal to one line; in given circle draw perpendicular diameters and repeatedly bisect an angle to get a small central angle smaller than twice angle LKM; join NC to obtain side of a regular inscribed polygon; use tangents and comparisons of ratios MK:LK > OC:OH > OP:OH to deduce ST:CN < MK:LK < F:LK and hence ST:CN < A:B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal magnitudes and a sector, it is possible to describe a polygon about the sector and to inscribe another in it so that the side of the circumscribed polygon may have to the side of the inscribed polygon a ratio less than the greater magnitude has to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same construction as Prop. 3 but bisect the angle of the sector repeatedly instead of a right angle between diameters; proof parallels that of Prop. 3. Note: the inscribed polygon uses the two bounding radii as two sides and other sides subtend equal parts of the sector's arc; the circumscribed polygon uses tangents parallel to the inscribed sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a circle and two unequal magnitudes, to describe a polygon about the circle and inscribe another in it, so that the circumscribed polygon may have to the inscribed a ratio less than the greater magnitude has to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take two unequal straight lines D, E with D:E < B:C (via Prop. 2), let F be a mean proportional between D and E; construct polygons as in Prop. 3 so that side ratio of circumscribed to inscribed < D:F. Duplicate ratio of sides equals ratio of areas (similar polygons), so area(Circumscribed):area(Inscribed) < D^2:F^2 = D:E, hence < B:C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal magnitudes and a sector, it is possible to circumscribe a polygon about the sector and inscribe in it another similar one so that the circumscribed may have to the inscribed a ratio less than the greater magnitude has to the less. Also, for a given circle or sector and certain area, by inscribing regular polygons successively one can leave segments whose total area is less than the given area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof parallels Prop. 5 and Prop. 3 constructions; by successive inscribing and taking remaining segments one can make remaining area arbitrarily small (reference to Euclid). Then construct circumscribed polygon so that area remaining between circumference and circumscribed figure is less than given area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 7
rubrics_metrics.description: If in an isosceles cone a pyramid be inscribed having an equilateral base, the surface of the pyramid excluding the base is equal to a triangle having its base equal to the perimeter of the base of the pyramid and its height equal to the perpendicular drawn from the apex on one side of the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because base sides are equal, perpendiculars from apex to all sides are equal; surface composed of congruent isosceles triangles whose altitudes equal that perpendicular; summing these triangles gives the claimed equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pyramid be circumscribed about an isosceles cone, the surface of the pyramid excluding its base is equal to a triangle having its base equal to the perimeter of the base of the pyramid and its height equal to the side (generator) of the cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base of pyramid is a polygon circumscribed about circle; line joining apex to point of contact is perpendicular to that side and equal to the cone generator; all such perpendiculars are equal, hence the surface equals the triangle as stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9
rubrics_metrics.description: If in the circular base of an isosceles cone a chord be placed, and from its extremities straight lines be drawn to the apex of the cone, the triangle so formed will be less than the portion of the surface of the cone intercepted between the lines drawn to the apex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bisect arc and consider triangles OAC, OBC and triangle OAB; let their area excess be D. Two cases: (I) D >= sum of corresponding surface segments => use inclusion-of-surfaces argument (Assumptions) to compare triangle areas and cone surface parts. (II) D less than sum => repeatedly bisect arcs to produce segments sum less than D and compare sums similarly; in both cases deduce AOAC+AOBC > AOAB and consequently triangle OAB < cone portion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10
rubrics_metrics.description: If in the plane of the circular base of an isosceles cone two tangents be drawn to the circle meeting in a point, and the points of contact and the point of concourse of the tangents be respectively joined to the apex of the cone, the sum of the two triangles formed by the joining lines and the two tangents are together greater than the included portion of the surface of the cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let AD, BD be tangents meeting at D; compare lengths AD+DB with AE+EF+FB (where EF tangent at middle point is parallel etc.). Use perpendicular generators and equality to translate line inequalities into triangle area inequalities. Consider G = excess; two cases: (I) G >= sum of segments between circle and tangents => inclusion of pyramid surface vs cone part gives inequality. (II) G < sum => bisect arcs and build polygon so remainders < G and proceed as in Prop. 9 to conclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane parallel to the axis of a right cylinder cut the cylinder, the part of the surface of the cylinder cut off by the plane is greater than the area of the parallelogram in which the plane cuts it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof follows method of Prop. 9 by comparing triangular/segmental pieces; omitted in text but reference given that method is identical to Props. 9 and 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 12
rubrics_metrics.description: If at the extremities of two generators of any right cylinder tangents be drawn to the circular bases in the planes of those bases respectively, and if the pairs of tangents meet, the parallelograms formed by each generator and the two corresponding tangents respectively are together greater than the included portion of the surface of the cylinder between the two generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof parallels that of Propositions 9 and 10 applied to cylinder; details omitted as analogous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribed vs Circumscribed solids comparison (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: From earlier properties: (1) if a pyramid be inscribed in an isosceles cone, the surface of the pyramid excluding the base is less than the surface of the cone excluding the base; (2) if a pyramid be circumscribed about an isosceles cone, the surface of the pyramid excluding the base is greater than that of the cone. Similarly for prisms and cylinders: inscribed prism surface less than cylinder surface; circumscribed prism surface greater than cylinder surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences follow from Propositions 7–12 and comparison/inclusion arguments used earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 13
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of any right cylinder excluding the bases is equal to a circle whose radius is a mean proportional between the side (a generator) of the cylinder and the diameter of its base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let base circle be A, diameter CD, height HF. Let H be mean proportional between CD and EF; circle B with radius H equals cylinder surface S. Proof by contradiction: assume B<S or B>S. In each case construct similar circumscribed/inscribed polygons about B and corresponding prisms about A; use similarity and area comparisons to derive contradictions, hence B = S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 14
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of any isosceles cone excluding the base is equal to a circle whose radius is a mean proportional between the side of the cone (a generator) and the radius of the circle which is the base of the cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let base radius C and generator D, let E be mean proportional; circle B radius E equals cone surface S. Proof by contradiction similar to Prop. 13: assume B<S or B>S, construct similar polygons and pyramids, compare polygonal areas, apply previous propositions to reach contradiction; conclude B = S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of any isosceles cone has the same ratio to its base as the side of the cone has to the radius of the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Prop. 14: since surface equals circle whose radius is mean proportional between side and radius, and areas of circles are proportional to squares of radii, the stated ratio relation holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 16
rubrics_metrics.description: If an isosceles cone be cut by a plane parallel to the base, the portion of the surface of the cone between the parallel planes is equal to a circle whose radius is a mean proportional between (1) the portion of the side of the cone intercepted by the parallel planes and (2) the line equal to the sum of the radii of the circles in the parallel planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider triangle through axis and its analogous cut triangles; apply Prop. 14 to show surfaces equal to circles with radii sqrt(OA·AC) and sqrt(OD·DF); difference equals circle with radius sqrt(DA·(AC+DF)) by algebraic manipulation using proportionalities OA:AC = OD:DF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Cones having equal height have the same ratio as their bases; and those having equal bases have the same ratio as their heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to Euclid: standard proportionality properties of cones and cylinders; used later in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cylinder be cut by a plane parallel to the base, then, as the cylinder is to the cylinder, so is the axis to the axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proportionality of similar cylinders (Euclid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3
rubrics_metrics.description: The cones which have the same bases as the cylinders (and equal height) are in the same ratio as the cylinders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportionality relation used to relate cone and cylinder measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 4
rubrics_metrics.description: The bases of equal cones are reciprocally proportional to their heights; and those cones whose bases are reciprocally proportional to their heights are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclidean proportionality result used in equality arguments for cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 5
rubrics_metrics.description: The cones, the diameters of whose bases have the same ratio as their axes, are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters of the bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard similarity/triplicate power relation for cones (reference to Euclid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 17
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be two isosceles cones, and the surface of one cone be equal to the base of the other, while the perpendicular from the centre of the base of the first cone on the side of that cone is equal to the height of the second, the cones will be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let triangle sections correspond; equality of base to surface and equality of the perpendicular and height give base ratios equal to surface:base ratios and hence by Lemma 4 the cones are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 18
rubrics_metrics.description: Any solid rhombus consisting of isosceles cones is equal to the cone which has its base equal to the surface of one of the cones composing the rhombus and its height equal to the perpendicular drawn from the apex of the second cone to one side of the first cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct auxiliary cones whose bases and heights are arranged to equate volumes via Lemma 1 and Prop. 15; show cones are equal by comparing bases and heights and using reciprocal proportionality, concluding rhombus equals the constructed cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 19
rubrics_metrics.description: If an isosceles cone be cut by a plane parallel to the base, and on the resulting circular section a cone be described having as its apex the centre of the base, and if the rhombus so formed be taken away from the whole cone, the part remaining will be equal to the cone with base equal to the surface of the portion of the first cone between the parallel planes and with height equal to the perpendicular drawn from the centre of the base of the first cone on one side of that cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct cones with bases equal to the surfaces and equal heights; use equality relations (Props. 17–18) and decomposition (cone = rhombus + remainder) to show the remainder equals the cone with stated base and height.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 20
rubrics_metrics.description: If one of the two isosceles cones forming a rhombus be cut by a plane parallel to the base and on the resulting circular section a cone be described having the same apex as the second cone, and if the resulting rhombus be taken from the whole rhombus, the remainder will be equal to the cone with base equal to the surface of the portion of the cone between the parallel planes and with height equal to the perpendicular drawn from the apex of the second cone to the side of the first cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous construction to Prop. 19 but the auxiliary cone uses the other apex; proceed by decomposing cones into cones of equal height and comparing bases to conclude equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 21
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular polygon of an even number of sides being inscribed in a circle so that AA' is a diameter, if two angular points next but one to each other, as B, B', be joined, and the other lines parallel to BB' joining pairs of angular points be drawn, then (BB + CC' + ...): AA' = A'B: BA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let BB', CC', ... meet AA' in points F, G, ...; using similar triangles BF:FA = B'F:FK and summing antecedents and consequents yields (BB'+CC'+...):AA' = BF:FA = A'B:BA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 22
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polygon be inscribed in a segment of a circle so that all its sides excluding the base are equal and their number even, and if lines parallel to the base joining pairs of angular points be drawn, then (BB' + CC' + ... + 21M): AM = A'B: BA, where M is midpoint of base and AM is diameter through M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join corresponding diagonals and apply similar-triangles relations BF:FA = B'F:FP = CG:PG etc.; summing gives (BB'+CC'+...+21M):AM = BF:FA = A'B:BA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 23
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a great circle of a sphere and inscribe in it a regular polygon whose sides are a multiple of four. Let AA', MM' be diameters at right angles and join opposite polygon vertices. Then if the polygon and great circle revolve about AA', the polygon vertices (except A,A') describe circles on the sphere perpendicular to AA'; the sides describe portions of conical surfaces; comparing hemisphere and the revolved inscribed figure shows the hemisphere's surface is greater than that of the inscribed figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric reasoning: the revolved inscribed figure lies entirely inside the hemisphere and shares the same planar boundary, both are concave same way; by Assumptions on surfaces the hemisphere is larger; extend to whole sphere by halves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24
rubrics_metrics.description: If a regular polygon (number of sides a multiple of four) be inscribed in a great circle and expanded by revolution about diameter AA', and if BB' be drawn subtending two sides and parallels to BB' be drawn joining pairs of points, then the surface of the inscribed revolved figure equals a circle whose square of radius equals the rectangle BA (BB' + CC' + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose the revolved surface into cones and frusta corresponding to BB', CC', ...; use Prop. 14 and 16 to express each part as a circle of radius sqrt(BA·(sum of parallels)) and sum to obtain the whole surface equal to that circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 25
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of the figure inscribed in the sphere as above (portions of conical surfaces) is less than four times the greatest circle in the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Prop. 21 identity (BB'+...):AA' = A'B:AB deduce AB(BB'+...)=AA'·A'B. Hence radius^2 of the equivalent circle R equals AA'·A'B < AA'^2, so radius(R) < 2·(radius of great circle), therefore area(R) < 4 times great circle area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 26
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure inscribed in the sphere (as above) is equal in volume to a cone whose base is a circle equal to the surface of the inscribed figure and whose height is equal to the perpendicular drawn from the centre of the sphere to one side of the polygon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct cones with apex at sphere centre whose bases are the circles on BB', CC', ... as diameters; each solid rhombus OBAB' equals a cone (Prop. 18); sum the cone-volumes (equal-height cones) to conclude total volume equals a cone with base equal to total surface and height equal to the perpendicular p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 27
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure inscribed in the sphere as before is less than four times the cone whose base is a great circle of the sphere and whose height is equal to the radius of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By Prop. 26 the inscribed solid has volume equal to a cone of base equal to the inscribed surface and height p (perpendicular); Prop. 25 bounds base < 4·great circle, and p < radius, hence cone volume < 4 times cone with great circle base and radius height.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 28
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a regular polygon (number of sides multiple of four) be circumscribed about a great circle and about the polygon describe another circle concentric with the great circle. Revolve about AA'. Then the circumscribed figure is greater than the sphere itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a side Bd touching the inner circle at K and its contact K'. The revolved region from the polygon includes the revolved circular segment about KK'; since polygonal revolved part entirely includes the segment and both concave same way, by Assumptions the circumscribed figure exceeds the sphere; apply to opposite side and sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 29
rubrics_metrics.description: In a figure circumscribed to a sphere as before, the surface is equal to a circle the square of whose radius is equal to AB(BB' + CC' + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the circumscribed figure is inscribed in a larger sphere, the proof of Prop. 24 applies verbatim to express its surface as a circle with radius satisfying the stated rectangle relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 30 (numbered 90 in text)
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of a figure circumscribed as before about a sphere is greater than four times the great circle of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let AB... be polygon of 4n sides circumscribing inner circle; using identity (BB'+...):AA' = A'B:AB get AB(BB'+...)=AA'·A'B, hence radius(R) = sqrt(AA'·A'B) > A'B. Since A'B equals twice the point-of-contact diameter, radius(R) > inner diameter, so surface R > 4·great circle area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 31 (numbered 91 in text)
rubrics_metrics.description: The solid of revolution circumscribed as before about a sphere is equal to a cone whose base is equal to the surface of the solid and whose height is equal to the radius of the sphere. Corollary: The solid circumscribed about the smaller sphere is greater than four times the cone whose base is a great circle of the sphere and whose height is equal to the radius of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The circumscribed solid is inscribed in a larger sphere; perpendiculars on any side of revolving polygon equal radius of inner sphere; by analogy to Prop. 26 the volume equals cone with base equal to surface and height radius. Combining with Prop. 30 yields the corollary on volume being > 4 times the reference cone.
